dayTitle: Two towns, one earthquake
title: The same event, recorded twice
task: Compare the two records from one earthquake
scene: Inês Cardoso has the vault record from the bench and the field station record from Bay Road. Same event, same minute, eleven hundred metres apart. One trace is short and sharp, the other is three times taller and goes on for half a minute longer.
question: What does the difference between the two records mean?
takeaway: A record describes one place, so two records of one earthquake can disagree and both be right.
why: Two nearby stations can record very different motion because the soil column between bedrock and the instrument changes the wavefield. Lower-velocity material and impedance contrasts can amplify some frequencies, while trapping, resonance and damping change both duration and spectral shape. That is more precise than saying soft soil simply makes every wave bigger. Here the Bay Road trace is both stronger and longer in the periods that matter to the Flats, so a real site effect fits the records far better than an eleven-hundred-metre source-distance difference.
assumes: an instrument records the shaking where it stands, not the earthquake itself

dayTitle: Two towns, one earthquake
title: Ground that people put there
task: Say what the ground under the Flats is made of
scene: Navarro has an 1892 survey and a photograph from 1948. Where Bay Road now runs there was a tidal creek, and the port was pumped into place out of the dredger over four summers.
question: Say what the ground under the Flats is made of
takeaway: Liquefaction needs susceptible soil, enough saturation and strong cyclic loading; young hydraulic fill often supplies the first two.
why: Hydraulic fill is often placed loose and below a shallow water table, which can make it vulnerable to liquefaction. During cyclic shaking, loose saturated grains try to rearrange. If water cannot drain quickly enough, pore-water pressure rises and effective stress at grain contacts falls; strength and stiffness can collapse temporarily. Age by itself is not a defence — some fills densify or drain, others remain susceptible for decades. The old creek line matters because the records and sand boils identify it as the wettest, weakest part of this deposit.
assumes: ground can be natural or placed by people

dayTitle: Two towns, one earthquake
title: Where the first day of assessment goes
task: Allocate six assessor-days so the plan can answer the re-occupancy question that matters today without spending the whole day on places where the decision is already made.
scene: Six assessors, two halves of a town and one day. Okonkwo wants them where the buildings are worst. Bram Halvorsen wants them where the most people are waiting to go home.
question: Allocate six assessor-days so the plan can answer the re-occupancy question that matters today without spending the whole day on places where the decision is already made.
takeaway: Send inspectors where the answer will change what happens next, not where the damage photographs best.
why: An inspection is worth what it changes. Four hundred households are sleeping in a hall waiting on a placard, and most of those buildings will come back green or yellow, so a day spent there sends hundreds of people home. Marina Court is already cordoned and already empty, so an assessment today changes nobody's night. The Parade is the same: the damage has happened, the street is shut, and knowing more about it this afternoon moves nothing. Damage is not the same as urgency.
assumes: an assessment programme is a queue, and the order is a decision
why_this_format: The stop already gives a finite team, one day, and several legitimate places to send them. ALLOCATE turns the priority argument into the actual trade-off: every assessor-day spent documenting an already-cordoned building is one that cannot resolve whether hundreds of households can go home. The player has to preserve the decision-changing question under a real capacity limit instead of merely selecting the most urgent-sounding location.
player_does: spend a pool of six assessor-days across the Flats terraces, Marina Court, Upper Town and the Parade
watch which operational questions the current allocation can actually answer before committing it
keep the Flats re-occupancy question answerable while deciding which lower-value question to forgo
trap_is_satisfied_by: The four inspection packages cost ten assessor-days against the six available. The required Flats re-occupancy question needs the four-day Flats package and cannot be answered by the existing cordons or closure orders alone; the Marina Court, Upper Town and Parade questions are explicitly optional.

protectedItems.label: Existing cordons and closure orders
protectedItems.note: They control known hazards but do not answer whether the Flats terraces can be re-occupied.

answers.label: Can the waiting Flats households be given an occupancy decision today?
Can Marina Court be described in more detail today?
Can the standing Upper Town houses receive an extra follow-up today?
Can the already-closed Parade be documented in more detail today?

answerText: Keep enough of the six assessor-days on the Flats terraces to resolve the re-occupancy decision for the households waiting to go home. Marina Court is already empty and cordoned, and the Parade is already closed; extra detail there is useful but not the question that changes the most people’s night.

failure_feedback.action: spending most of the day on Marina Court or the Parade
failure_feedback.consequence: the team learns more about damage whose immediate control is already in place while the Flats households remain without an occupancy decision
failure_feedback.line: Damage is not the same thing as urgency.

dayTitle: The number everybody has already heard
title: How far away it started
task: Locate the source from arrival times
scene: The vault trace shows the P arrival at 04:12:19 and the S arrival at 04:12:32. Cardoso wants the distance before anybody draws a circle on a map.
question: Estimate the distance from this station to the source.
takeaway: The gap between the two arrivals grows with distance, so one station gives a distance and three give a place.
why: Both waves leave at the same instant and travel the same path, but the P wave is faster, so the gap between their arrivals is a clock that has been running since the earthquake started. For shallow crust the two speeds work out at roughly eight kilometres for every second of gap. One station turns that into a radius and knows only that the source is somewhere on a circle; three stations turn three circles into a point, which is why a network exists at all.
assumes: P waves travel faster than S waves through the same rock

dayTitle: The number everybody has already heard
title: Why the number moved
task: Explain what changed between the 6.6 and 6.8 solutions
scene: Tanaka has both agency bulletins on the desk. The early one used the first stations to report; the later one used the whole network and the long-period part of the record.
question: Which explanation of the 6.6-to-6.8 revision is scientifically defensible?
takeaway: A magnitude revision means the estimate changed as the available waveform and network coverage improved; the earthquake itself did not change.
why: Rapid magnitude solutions use the stations and waveform windows available in the first minutes. A later moment-magnitude solution can use more stations, longer records and a better-constrained source model. That later estimate can move either up or down; revision is not evidence that the earthquake changed or that the first agency was careless. The scale is logarithmic, too: a 0.2-unit change is modest in magnitude but corresponds to roughly a factor of two in the usual radiated-energy scaling, not a two-percent adjustment.
assumes: a magnitude is computed from records, so more records can change it

dayTitle: The number everybody has already heard
title: A notice somebody acts on
task: Say it in a way that survives being repeated
scene: Adeyemi has two hundred words and an audience that has heard two numbers and a rumour about a bigger one coming. She wants to know what the notice has to contain.
question: Say it in a way that survives being repeated
takeaway: A notice earns its place by changing what somebody does, and everything else in it competes with that.
why: People act on the first thing they can use, so the action goes first: what to do about the building you are standing outside. The reason comes next, because a reason is what makes an instruction survive being repeated by somebody else. The magnitude revision belongs third — it matters, but nobody does anything differently because of it — and the aftershock forecast last, framed as a rate, because it is the part most likely to be misread as a prediction of a particular event.
assumes: a public notice is read once, quickly, by somebody who is tired

dayTitle: What the placard is claiming
title: Six minutes outside a building
task: Say what a rapid assessment actually samples
scene: Whitcombe's form has eleven boxes and a place for the colour. He filled four hundred of them in two days, and he has kept a second list of everything he did not look at.
question: Say what a rapid assessment actually samples
takeaway: A rapid assessment is triage: it records observed hazards and access limits, not a complete structural evaluation.
why: A rapid assessment is designed to screen many buildings quickly after a disaster. It can identify gross leaning, collapse hazards, obvious structural distress and accessible life-safety problems. It cannot establish the condition of concealed connections, inaccessible rooms, foundations or every member in the load path. The discipline is therefore two-part: record what was observed and record what could not be observed. A green placard is useful only when later users do not silently expand its scope beyond the inspection that produced it.
assumes: an inspection covers what the inspector could see

dayTitle: What the placard is claiming
title: Green does not mean safe
task: Explain what green means to somebody standing in the street
scene: Delacroix has three residents outside with green placards and one question between them: is my house all right? Adeyemi will not say yes and needs a sentence that is not a dodge.
question: What does a green placard entitle somebody to be told?
takeaway: A placard is an occupancy decision based on a defined inspection, not a warranty that every hidden part is undamaged.
why: The useful public message is specific: the rapid inspection found no condition requiring an occupancy restriction in the areas and features that could be assessed, and the form records important limitations. That is different from promising the building is undamaged, fully evaluated or safe against every aftershock. The distinction is not legalistic hedging; it tells the owner what the inspection actually bought and which unresolved areas may still need follow-up before a particular use resumes.
assumes: people read a colour as a verdict

dayTitle: What the placard is claiming
title: The ones worth a second visit
task: Decide which buildings get looked at again
scene: Two engineers are free tomorrow. Tanaka lays out four candidates from the four hundred, each of which somebody has asked about.
question: Which building gets the detailed evaluation first?
takeaway: Re-inspect where the first look was least able to see and the consequence of being wrong is largest.
why: Two things decide this: how much the first inspection could not see, and what it costs to be wrong. The hospital is worst on both. It has ninety people inside it now, it is holding a yellow that nobody can resolve without opening the plant room, and every day it stays yellow is a day the district's care is running somewhere else. The red warehouse is empty and already restricted, so nothing changes today. The two green buildings are low consequence, and anxiety, while real, is a reason for a phone call rather than for an engineer.
assumes: a second inspection is a scarce thing to spend

dayTitle: The building that looks worst
title: The raft is fine and the building is not
task: Which explanation fits every observation?
scene: Navarro's survey: the raft is intact, level within itself, and rotated. One side has gone down 340 millimetres and the other has come up 90. The sand fans are worst on the low side.
question: Which explanation fits every observation?
takeaway: A structure can fail without anything in the structure breaking.
why: The observations point to support beneath the raft rather than distortion within the frame. The raft is intact and the building rotated almost as a rigid body; one edge settled while the other heaved, with fresh sand ejecta concentrated on the low side. During liquefaction, excess pore pressure can sharply reduce effective stress and bearing resistance, allowing settlement and lateral movement without the frame itself yielding. That does not prove every detail, but it is the hypothesis that explains the survey, ejecta and undamaged frame together.
assumes: a foundation spreads a building's weight into the ground

dayTitle: The building that looks worst
title: What eight degrees does
task: Decide what the lean actually costs
scene: Okonkwo has the column loads. At eight degrees the weight above each column no longer lands over its centre, and the offset grows with height up the building.
question: What is the engineering objection to leaving Marina Court standing?
takeaway: The lean matters because gravity now acts with eccentricity, creating P–Δ effects and extra bending demand in the frame.
why: A column is efficient when its gravity load stays close to its axis. Once the building leans, the weight above acts with an offset, creating additional bending moment; as lateral displacement grows, the gravity load can amplify that demand through P–Δ effects. The engineering question is therefore not whether eight degrees looks frightening, but whether the measured geometry, member capacities and continued ground stability leave adequate margin. The undamaged frame is encouraging evidence, not permission to ignore the new load path.
assumes: a leaning column carries its load off-centre

dayTitle: The building that looks worst
title: What knocking it down would fix
task: Spend five investigation-days on the evidence that would most change what the town does about Marina Court and the twelve neighbouring blocks.
scene: Halvorsen wants it gone this week. Delacroix points out that the twelve buildings around it stand on the same ground, and nobody is proposing to demolish those.
question: Spend five investigation-days on the evidence that would most change what the town does about Marina Court and the twelve neighbouring blocks.
takeaway: Demolishing the visible case leaves the condition that produced it, and the condition is under the whole street.
why: Demolition would remove the hazard posed by Marina Court but would not explain or change the ground beneath the neighbouring blocks. Because the same fill extends along the street, the decision that generalises is a targeted geotechnical investigation — CPTs, boreholes and groundwater information — while the leaning building remains cordoned and monitored. Underpinning or straightening may eventually be appropriate, and demolition may still be chosen for cost or residual risk. The key is not to confuse removing the most visible symptom with learning which sites share its cause.
assumes: a decision can treat a symptom or a cause
why_this_format: The decision is not simply demolish versus do not demolish. The updated lesson says the valuable measurement is the one that generalises from one visibly failed building to the rest of the street. VALUE makes that distinction operational: the player has a limited investigation budget and must buy evidence that can change the town-wide ground decision rather than spend it all refining a symptom whose immediate hazard is already controlled.
player_does: compare four proposed uses of a limited investigation window
inspect what decision each proposal could change for Marina Court and for neighbouring buildings
spend the budget on the evidence that tests whether the ground condition extends across the Flats
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented authoring costs: the four options total twelve investigation-days against a five-day budget. The three-day corridor ground campaign is decisive because it addresses the shared ground mechanism; monitoring, demolition planning and a one-building underpinning concept all answer narrower axes and cannot establish which neighbouring blocks share the cause.

options.label: CPTs, boreholes and groundwater checks across the Flats corridor
Advance demolition engineering for Marina Court
Develop an underpinning concept for Marina Court alone

answerText: Buy the corridor-wide ground investigation. Marina Court still needs its cordon and monitoring, but CPTs, boreholes and groundwater information are the evidence that can tell the town whether the same failure mechanism threatens the surrounding blocks. Demolishing or underpinning one building does not answer that question.

failure_feedback.action: spending the investigation window on demolition planning alone
failure_feedback.consequence: the visible leaning building can be removed while the town learns nothing about whether the same susceptible ground extends under the twelve neighbouring blocks
failure_feedback.line: That fixes the building everybody can see, not the condition under the street.

dayTitle: The one everybody assumed was fine
title: A hall with nothing in the middle
task: Build the lateral load path from the precast panel to the ground, then name the link that governs whether the panel stays attached.
scene: The gym is 34 metres across with a steel truss roof and precast concrete side panels. The classrooms next door are small rooms with walls every four metres and no damage at all.
question: Build the lateral load path from the precast panel to the ground, then name the link that governs whether the panel stays attached.
takeaway: A long-span hall depends on a complete lateral load path; the small connections between large components can govern the whole system.
why: The classroom block has many short, redundant paths from roof and walls into the foundations. The gym has a long roof diaphragm that must collect lateral inertia, deliver it to resisting walls or frames, and keep heavy precast panels attached while everything moves. Any weak link can break the path. That makes the roof-to-panel and diaphragm connections high-priority details, but it does not make the panels themselves automatically adequate — every component still has to be checked for the demand it actually receives.
assumes: a horizontal force has to travel through a building to reach the ground
why_this_format: This stop is already a transfer-path problem. CHAIN makes the player assemble the force route instead of matching prose descriptions: panel inertia has to cross a small roof connection, enter the roof diaphragm, reach the resisting end wall and finally the foundation. The large visible members are deliberately distracting; the reasoning is to find the small connection whose failure breaks an otherwise strong path.
player_does: arrange the components in the order the panel’s horizontal inertia must travel to reach the ground
separate the large obvious members from the link that actually transfers force between them
name the roof-to-panel tie as the governing link before seeing the verdict
trap_is_satisfied_by: The large precast panel body is the authored distractor, while the governing roof-to-panel tie is a different element and appears second in the correct transfer path rather than first.

elements.label: Horizontal inertia of the precast panel
elements.transfers: the panel’s own mass responding to the shaking — the force everything after this has to carry

elements.label: Tie between the precast panel and the roof
elements.transfers: panel inertia across the joint into the roof, and holds the panel on out of plane

elements.label: Roof diaphragm carrying force toward the end wall
elements.transfers: the collected roof and panel inertia along the roof, in its own plane, to the end walls

elements.label: Resisting end wall / frame
elements.transfers: in-plane shear from the diaphragm down to its own base

elements.label: Foundation and ground
elements.transfers: base shear from the resisting elements into the ground

elements.label: The large precast panel body
elements.transfers: in-plane shear down its own length, once something has delivered force to it

answerText: The panel’s inertia has to cross the panel-to-roof tie, enter the roof diaphragm, reach a resisting end wall or frame, and then reach the foundation. The governing link is the small tie between the panel and roof: if it lets go, the size of the panel and roof does not preserve the load path.

failure_feedback.action: naming the precast panel itself as the governing element
failure_feedback.consequence: the panel can remain strong in its own plane while its small attachment fails and the lateral load path opens
failure_feedback.line: The biggest piece is not automatically the weak link.

dayTitle: The one everybody assumed was fine
title: What the tested anchors actually carried
task: Compare the measured anchor capacity with the estimated earthquake demand
scene: Kirsten Sørensen has pulled two cast-in anchors from a spare panel in the yard. The design drawing says 40 kilonewtons each. The first came out at 24, the second at 27.
question: Estimate the observed capacity-to-demand ratio for the two tested anchors.
takeaway: Two pull tests can show a serious capacity shortfall; they do not by themselves establish a code-level factor of safety for every anchor in the building.
why: The two tests average 25.5 kN against an assessed demand of 31 kN, giving an observed capacity-to-demand ratio of about 0.82. That identifies a problem: these specimens did not demonstrate capacity above the estimated demand. Calling 0.82 a formal factor of safety would overstate what two tests establish, because design checks include variability, failure mode and resistance factors. The practical conclusion is simpler: restrict the gym, obtain representative testing and design a repair before the connection is relied on again.
assumes: a designed capacity is a claim to be checked

dayTitle: The one everybody assumed was fine
title: Four hundred children on Monday
task: Say what happens to term
scene: The classrooms are sound and the gym is not. Halvorsen points out that a school without a hall is still a school, and that a district without a school is four hundred families who cannot work.
question: What should happen to Bay Road School on Monday?
takeaway: The useful question is which parts can be occupied, not whether the site is open or shut.
why: The useful decision is component-specific. The classroom block has no identified structural deficiency, while the gym has heavy panels attached by connections whose tested capacity is below the estimated demand. If the gym can be physically isolated from classroom access and egress, the classrooms can reopen while the hall remains closed and the connections are repaired. If routes or falling hazards overlap, that separation has to be solved first. Partial occupancy is not optimism; it is a controlled use tied to the actual defect.
assumes: a building can be used in part

dayTitle: The hospital, and what waiting costs
title: The part nobody has seen
task: You have time for one direct verification before the hospital placard review. Choose which recorded claim to verify.
scene: Three days of inspection have cleared the frame, the cladding and the stairs. What is left is a plant room on the roof, holding two water tanks, that nobody has opened.
question: You have time for one direct verification before the hospital placard review. Choose which recorded claim to verify.
takeaway: When most of a building is resolved, the placard is being held by whatever is left, and it is worth naming precisely.
why: A yellow placard is not a fog: it is one or more specific unresolved items, and the discipline is to write them down until the list is short enough to finish. Frame, cladding and stairs are cleared and cannot be what is holding this. Two full water tanks on a roof are a large mass in the worst possible place, and their restraint has not been seen. That is the item. Naming it turns four days of general anxiety into one afternoon with a ladder and a torch.
assumes: a building's parts can be cleared separately
why_this_format: The lesson is that a cleared box on a form is not the same thing as a condition that was actually observed. ATTEST turns the unresolved-items list into the work itself. Three important claims already have direct inspection behind them; the roof plant-room claim does not. With only one verification available, rechecking a comfortable backed claim wastes the opportunity to resolve the item that is actually holding the placard.
player_does: open the evidence attached to the frame, cladding, stairs and roof plant-room claims
spend the single verification visit on one claim
decide whether the placard can be revisited after the previously inaccessible item is directly observed
trap_is_satisfied_by: There are four claims but only one verification visit. The roof plant-room restraint is critical and unbacked and fits within the budget; the stair/egress claim is also critical but already backed by direct inspection, satisfying the requirement that not every critical claim be unverified.

claims.label: The reinforced-concrete frame has no observed condition requiring the current restriction
claims.verification: Three days of frame inspection on all accessible floors.

claims.label: The external cladding does not present the unresolved structural issue
claims.verification: Cladding inspection completed on day two.

claims.label: The main stair and egress route are usable for the proposed occupancy
claims.verification: Stair core inspected first because it is the escape route.

claims.label: The roof water-tank restraints are adequate for the proposed occupancy
claims.verification: Open the roof plant room and directly inspect the two tank restraints.

answerText: Verify the roof plant room. The frame, cladding and stairs already have direct observations behind them; the two full water tanks and their restraints are the critical condition nobody has seen. The placard is being held by that specific unbacked claim, not by a general lack of information about the hospital.

failure_feedback.action: using the one verification visit to recheck the frame or stairs
failure_feedback.consequence: the review gains more evidence for a claim that was already backed while the critical roof-tank restraint remains unobserved
failure_feedback.line: The open item is the room nobody has entered.

dayTitle: The hospital, and what waiting costs
title: What four more days buys
task: Put the cost of waiting into the same units
scene: Tanaka has the aftershock rate for the coming week. Ives has the transfer log. Halvorsen wants both of them stated as consequences rather than as principles.
question: How should the office weigh four more days of evidence-gathering?
takeaway: A decision to wait is a decision with an outcome, and it has to be compared with the outcome of deciding now.
why: Both sides of the decision have consequences and both can be estimated. Delay carries transfers, postponed care and operational strain. Additional testing is worthwhile when it has a realistic chance of changing the safety decision. Here the frame has already been inspected and the unresolved item is the unvisited roof plant room with heavy tanks; a four-day coring programme answers a different question. The disciplined test is therefore value of information: what decision could this evidence change, how likely is that, and what is paid while waiting for it?
assumes: a delay has consequences that can be counted

dayTitle: The hospital, and what waiting costs
title: The instrument in the basement
task: Check what the hospital actually experienced
scene: There is an accelerograph in the hospital basement, installed in 1998 and never used in anger. Cardoso has the record. It shows a peak of 0.31 g, and the building was designed for 0.35.
question: What can the 0.31 g basement record legitimately add to the assessment?
takeaway: A building-mounted accelerograph measures one part of the demand directly; it does not turn a code design value into a damage threshold.
why: The basement instrument removes major uncertainty about the motion at this site: peak base acceleration was 0.31 g. Comparing that with the 0.35 g design input is useful context, but a code design value is not a tripwire below which damage is impossible. Structural demand also depends on frequency content, duration, ductility, detailing and component response. The record therefore shows that base acceleration was not obviously beyond the nominal design input, while the plant-room restraint and observed-condition inspection remain separate questions.
assumes: a building can be instrumented, and the record is about that building

dayTitle: What the ground will do next
title: The rate, falling
task: Fit the decay and say what it predicts
scene: Day one had 96 events above magnitude 3. Day two had 52, day three 41, day four 26. Tanaka's fit has the rate roughly halving as the elapsed time doubles.
question: Estimate the number of magnitude 3+ aftershocks on day eight.
takeaway: A simple Omori-style decay gives a central rate estimate; the real forecast also needs uncertainty around that curve.
why: A simple Omori-style model has aftershock rate fall approximately as an inverse power of time after the mainshock. With p near one, doubling elapsed time roughly halves the central expected rate, so 26 events around day four suggests roughly 13 around day eight. Real sequences scatter around that curve and fitted parameters have uncertainty, so thirteen is not a quota for the day. The model is useful because it turns a decaying sequence into an expected rate and range that staffing and inspection decisions can use.
assumes: a rate can fall smoothly without ever reaching zero

dayTitle: What the ground will do next
title: A rate is not a schedule
task: Say what a forecast does not claim
scene: The notice draft says the aftershocks will have stopped by the end of the month. Cardoso points at the sentence and asks where the month came from.
question: What can the forecast honestly say?
takeaway: A rate says how often, not when or how large, and writing it as a date makes a promise nobody can keep.
why: The fit gives a rate and an uncertainty on that rate, and nothing else. It cannot give an end date, because a power law fades rather than stops. It cannot rule out a large event — the magnitudes in a sequence follow their own distribution, and a bigger one is always possible and always less likely. And it cannot promise that each day is safer, because the rate is an average and the sequence is random around it. Everything the forecast can say is still useful, and the useful part is a number per week.
assumes: a forecast states what is expected on average

dayTitle: What the ground will do next
title: Damaged, and waiting to be asked again
task: Say what the falling rate means for a cracked building
scene: Okonkwo has eleven buildings with cracked shear walls that are still standing. Each has less capacity than it had a week ago, and the sequence has not finished.
question: Why does a falling aftershock rate still leave these eleven buildings urgent?
takeaway: Damage lowers the capacity, so the same aftershock that was survivable last week may not be this week.
why: Risk is hazard against capacity, and the earthquake moved both. The hazard is falling with the sequence, which is the good news. But a cracked shear wall may have lost a third of what it could carry, and the shaking that would now be enough to hurt it is far more common than the shaking that damaged it. A magnitude 5 aftershock is many times more likely than another 6.8, and against a weakened building it is the one that matters. That is why the eleven get shored this week rather than next month.
assumes: a damaged element carries less than it used to

dayTitle: The material, and what it can still carry
title: A number, with a method attached
task: Get a strength from a damaged column
scene: Four cores, 100 mm across, cut from the cracked columns. Sørensen caps and crushes them: 28, 31, 24 and 30 megapascals. The 1974 drawing calls for 25.
question: What is the strongest claim these four core results support?
takeaway: Core tests characterize sampled concrete; they do not certify the residual capacity of the cracked columns.
why: The four cores are 28, 31, 24 and 30 MPa, centred near the 25 MPa specified strength. With only four specimens and one result below 25, the careful conclusion is not that every column exceeds design strength; it is that grossly weak concrete is not an obvious explanation for the damage. Member capacity is a different question because it also depends on reinforcement, confinement, bond, geometry and the damage state. The cores narrow the diagnosis; they do not clear the columns.
assumes: concrete strength is measured by crushing a sample of known size

dayTitle: The material, and what it can still carry
title: Which way the cracks run
task: Which explanation fits the pattern?
scene: The cracks run diagonally, in both directions, crossing each other in an X across the middle third of each column. They are fine, numerous and evenly spaced.
question: Which explanation fits the pattern?
takeaway: Crack geometry is diagnostic evidence: crossed diagonal cracking is consistent with reversing shear, but it does not by itself quantify remaining capacity.
why: Diagonal cracking is consistent with principal tension produced by shear, and crossed diagonals fit load reversals during earthquake shaking. The pattern is therefore much more consistent with cyclic shear demand than with simple long-term settlement or axial crushing. Fine, distributed cracks can indicate that reinforcement is controlling crack widths rather than allowing one brittle split, but that is not the same as proving the column is safe. Crack pattern identifies a likely mechanism; residual capacity still needs an engineering check.
assumes: a crack runs across the direction of the tension that opened it

dayTitle: The material, and what it can still carry
title: Part of a building, for part of a purpose
task: Decide what the building may be used for meanwhile
scene: The library is the only hall in the district big enough for the public meeting on Monday, and three of its ground-floor columns are cracked in shear.
question: Decide what the building may be used for meanwhile
takeaway: Restricted use is a real option between open and shut, and it has to name what the restriction is protecting against.
why: Restricted use only means something if the restriction matches the defect. The defect is load capacity in three ground-floor columns, so the first move is to take load off them, which means shoring. Then limit what goes back on: numbers, not areas, because it is weight and crowd movement that matter here. Then the time limit, so the restriction expires rather than becoming permanent by neglect. The public meeting is last because it is the use, and the use is decided by what the first three steps allow — not the other way round.
assumes: occupancy can be limited by number, by area or by time

dayTitle: The cordon nobody can lift
title: Three reasons wearing one line
task: Say what each part of the cordon is for
scene: Delacroix walks the boundary with the log. The northern arc is under the Parade's parapets. The eastern leg follows the gas main. The southern leg has no note against it at all.
question: Say what each part of the cordon is for
takeaway: Every part of a cordon should name the hazard it answers, or it cannot be lifted when that hazard goes.
why: A cordon lifts hazard by hazard, and that only works if somebody wrote down which hazard each stretch answers. Under the Parade the hazard is overhead and it ends when the parapets are taken down or tied back. On the gas main it ends when the utility signs the line off. On the liquefied street the hazard is not falling masonry at all — it is a road that cannot carry a fire appliance, which is about access rather than about danger to somebody walking. And the southern leg has no reason recorded, which means it is being held because it was drawn, and that is the one to look at first.
assumes: a boundary can be drawn for more than one reason

dayTitle: The cordon nobody can lift
title: Soft ground, three days on
task: Say whether the liquefied street is dangerous or just unusable
scene: Thandi Mbeki has been on Ferry Street with a hand auger. The sand fans have dried, the water table has dropped back, and the surface bears a person easily and a truck not at all.
question: What is the defensible status of Ferry Street now?
takeaway: Liquefaction is transient, but the ground left behind can have settlement, voids and uncertain bearing capacity even after pore pressure dissipates.
why: Liquefaction itself requires elevated pore pressure during shaking; that excess pressure dissipates afterward and grain contacts recover. What remains can include settlement, lateral spreading, ejecta, local voids and highly variable stiffness or bearing capacity. Loose sands can even densify during the process, so calling the whole deposit simply 'looser' is not justified. A person standing on the surface proves very little about truck support. The correct operational status is therefore disturbed ground with heavy-load capacity unverified and renewed liquefaction still possible in susceptible saturated layers during a strong aftershock.
assumes: liquefied ground regains strength as pore pressure dissipates

dayTitle: The cordon nobody can lift
title: A condition, not a date
task: Set what has to be true for people to go home
scene: Halvorsen wants a date. Delacroix wants a condition. Tanaka points out that a date makes a promise about the ground and a condition makes a promise about the office.
question: What should the office commit to?
takeaway: Tie a decision to a condition somebody can check, and it stays honest whatever the ground does next.
why: A date is a promise about the world, and the office does not control the world. A condition is a promise about the office, which is the thing it can keep — and publishing the list turns a wait into something residents can watch progress on, which is most of what people are asking for when they ask for a date. The aftershock rate is the wrong trigger because it is not the hazard on any of these streets, and waiting for detailed assessment of every building means nobody goes home for a month.
assumes: a commitment can be tied to a date or to an event

dayTitle: The photograph that changed the meeting
title: A real crack, and an unknown building
task: Say what the photograph establishes
scene: The photograph shows a column with a horizontal crack about a metre above the floor, in a basement with pipework and no daylight. There is no scale in the frame and no way to tell which column it is.
question: What has the photograph established?
takeaway: An authenticated photograph can establish an observation while leaving scale, location, age and mechanism unresolved.
why: Once the image is accepted as genuine, the crack is evidence — but evidence with narrow scope. Without scale, exact location, prior photographs or surrounding details, it cannot establish width, age, structural importance or cause. It does establish something operationally important: a basement area was outside the rapid inspection even though the building was green-placarded. The correct response is neither dismissal nor immediate evacuation from the photograph alone; it is to obtain the missing context quickly enough to decide whether the observation changes occupancy.
assumes: a photograph records what was in front of the lens

dayTitle: The photograph that changed the meeting
title: Down there with a torch
task: Choose the leading hypothesis and the check that would distinguish it
scene: In the basement: the crack is 0.4 mm and horizontal, a metre above the floor. Five more columns along the row carry one that looks the same.
question: What is the best-supported explanation to test first?
takeaway: A repeated pattern can identify the best hypothesis, but a plausible construction joint still has to be verified before it is called harmless.
why: A horizontal feature of nearly identical height and width across six columns strongly suggests a construction detail shared by all six, such as the top of a concrete lift. That is more likely than six independent shear failures producing the same geometry. But earthquake damage can also exploit construction joints, so 'construction joint' is a hypothesis, not an automatic clearance. Check drawings or pour records, inspect displacement and spalling across the joint, and compare with undamaged columns before deciding whether the earthquake changed its condition.
assumes: a defect that repeats in a pattern usually has a construction cause

dayTitle: The photograph that changed the meeting
title: The meeting
task: Say it at six o'clock
scene: Two hundred people, one photograph everybody has seen, and an office that has to explain both what it found tonight and why it did not find it on day one.
question: Say it at six o'clock
takeaway: Say what was found, what it means and what the process missed, in that order, and commit to the part you control.
why: The finding goes first because that is what everybody came for, and because withholding it while explaining process reads as evasion. Its meaning comes second: a construction joint rather than earthquake damage, which is the substance. Third is the honest part about the gap — the basement was never inspected, it was written down at the time, and nobody acted on the list. Last is what changes, because a commitment only lands after people believe the first three. Reversing any of this is how a meeting becomes an argument about the office instead of about the building.
assumes: trust is affected by how a process handles being wrong

dayTitle: A quiet day on the bench
title: Walls that fall outward
task: Say why the masonry failed the way it did
scene: On the Parade, every parapet came down into the street and no wall fell inward. The buildings behind them are undamaged, and their timber floors are still connected.
question: Why did the parapets fall and the walls below them stay?
takeaway: Unreinforced masonry fails out of plane, so the free top of a wall goes first and the tied part stays.
why: A masonry wall out of plane is only as good as what holds it. Where the floors meet it, the wall is tied back every few metres and cannot go far. Above the roof line there is nothing: the parapet is a free-standing cantilever of heavy brick with no tension capacity, and shaking is exactly the load it cannot take. Height does amplify the motion a little, and the parapet is thinner, but neither of those is the reason — a tied parapet of the same brick and the same thickness stays up.
assumes: masonry is strong in compression and weak in tension

dayTitle: A quiet day on the bench
title: What you can learn without breaking it
task: Spend the listed-façade disturbance allowance on the test that can actually support an anchor design.
scene: Ferreira has four options for the Parade's brickwork, and the owners have made it clear that cutting large holes in a listed façade is not one of them.
question: Spend the listed-façade disturbance allowance on the test that can actually support an anchor design.
takeaway: Choose the least destructive test that still answers the question you actually have.
why: The question is not how strong the brick is; it is whether an anchor drilled into this particular old wall will hold when the parapet tries to leave. That is exactly what a pull-out test on a trial anchor measures, in the real material, at the real depth, and it leaves a hole the size of the anchor. Crushing bricks answers a question nobody asked and destroys listed fabric to do it. The hammer and the penknife are useful for a general sense of condition, and neither produces a capacity anyone can design against.
assumes: a test can be destructive, semi-destructive or neither
why_this_format: The stop is explicitly about buying the measurement that answers the real design question while preserving a listed wall. VALUE makes the cost of irrelevant rigor visible. A destructive brick-strength test can produce a precise number and still fail to answer whether a tie anchor will pull out of this masonry; the trial-anchor pull-out test measures the property the retrofit actually depends on with much less fabric damage.
player_does: compare each proposed test by what property it measures and how much listed fabric it disturbs
spend a fixed disturbance allowance before seeing any result
choose the trial-anchor pull-out test because it directly measures the capacity the tie-back design needs
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented authoring disturbance costs: the four tests total 5.3 fabric-impact points against a one-point allowance. The one-point trial-anchor pull-out is decisive; the more destructive brick-core option measures a different axis, while the nearly non-destructive rebound and mortar surveys provide context but no anchor capacity.

options.label: Pull-out test on a trial anchor in the existing brickwork
Cut masonry samples for compressive testing
Visual and penknife survey of mortar joints

answerText: Use the disturbance allowance on a trial-anchor pull-out test. It measures the capacity the proposed tie-back actually needs, in the real wall and at the real embedment. Brick crushing, rebound hardness and mortar condition can all be informative, but none of them is the anchor capacity the retrofit must be designed against.

failure_feedback.consequence: listed fabric is removed to measure a material property that does not tell the engineer how much load a tie anchor can transfer into the existing wall
failure_feedback.line: A precise answer to the wrong question is still the wrong test.

dayTitle: A quiet day on the bench
title: Before the next one
task: Decide what is worth doing now
scene: Nothing on the Parade is dangerous today. The same parapets, on the same walls, will be here for the next earthquake, and the recurrence interval on this fault is about 140 years.
question: Decide what is worth doing now
takeaway: Fix a repeatedly observed, low-cost life-safety failure mode while access is already in place; do not let an average recurrence interval become a countdown clock.
why: Tying parapets back has an unusually strong case: the failure mode occurred repeatedly, the retrofit acts directly on it, and scaffolding already in place makes the marginal cost much lower. The quoted 140-year recurrence interval is not a promise of 140 quiet years after this event; earthquakes do not reset a calendar. That statistic belongs in long-term hazard context, not in the argument for waiting. Act now because the defect is known, the consequence is falling masonry, and the cheapest access window is open.
assumes: a hazard that has occurred will occur again

dayTitle: The record that was wrong all along
title: Measuring against the wrong zero
task: Say what a mis-sited reference does
scene: Cardoso has a temporary instrument on competent outcropping rock two hundred metres away, running beside the vault for five days. Across eleven aftershocks, the vault is about 1.6 times higher in the period band used for the Flats comparison.
question: What does the vault's own amplification do to the fortnight's numbers?
takeaway: A reference station is part of the measurement; if its site response is wrong, every ratio that uses it inherits that bias.
why: The Flats-to-vault amplification was a ratio with the vault in the denominator. If the vault itself amplifies motion by about 1.6 in the relevant period band, an observed ratio near three becomes roughly 3 × 1.6 ≈ 4.8 relative to competent rock. The correction is frequency-dependent, not a multiplier for every seismic quantity. The Flats recordings remain valid, and network magnitudes use many stations and source modelling. What must be revisited are site-response conclusions that explicitly treated this vault as unamplified rock.
assumes: a comparison is only as good as the thing compared against

dayTitle: The record that was wrong all along
title: What still stands
task: Sort the fortnight's conclusions
scene: Navarro puts four of the fortnight's conclusions on the board and asks which of them leaned on the vault ratio and which did not.
question: Sort the fortnight's conclusions
takeaway: A bad reference invalidates what was measured against it and leaves what was measured directly alone.
why: Trace each conclusion to its evidence. The Flats amplification ratio directly used the vault as its reference, so it must be restated. Marina Court's diagnosis came from settlement, heave, ejecta and structural survey; the hospital's 0.31 g came from its own basement instrument; and the parapet case rests on observed building failures and restraint details. Those conclusions may deserve other checks, but this particular reference-station error does not erase them. Dependency tracing is the point: one bad denominator should not become an excuse to discard unrelated evidence.
assumes: a conclusion can rest on one measurement or on several

dayTitle: The record that was wrong all along
title: Five times, not three
task: Decide what a bigger amplification changes
scene: If the Flats amplify by five rather than three, the shaking a future earthquake will deliver there is much larger than the figure in the district plan.
question: What does the corrected amplification change?
takeaway: Correcting site response changes forward-looking hazard and design assumptions; it does not rewrite damage that was observed directly.
why: Placards were based on observed building conditions, so they do not automatically change when a regional site-amplification ratio is corrected. Forward-looking work does: the Flats site-response model, design spectrum or site factors used for rebuilding, and the value placed on ground improvement all need reassessment. A single scalar amplification is not itself a complete design spectrum, especially because response varies with frequency. The correction changes what engineers should assume about future demand, not the magnitude of the earthquake that already occurred or the cracks already inspected.
assumes: design values are chosen from expected shaking

dayTitle: Three things at once
title: Which of the three cannot wait
task: Take one incident yourself and delegate the other two. Every handoff needs an owner, a first action and a return condition.
scene: Halvorsen has three incidents on the whiteboard and four engineers available. The water is still running, the aftershock has ended, and the school deadline is approaching. He wants the first ten minutes assigned, not a slogan about priorities.
question: Take one incident yourself and delegate the other two. Every handoff needs an owner, a first action and a return condition.
takeaway: In simultaneous incidents, stop the active hazard first while reserving enough people to check consequences that could make occupied buildings unsafe.
why: The burst main is the only hazard actively worsening minute by minute and can be arrested quickly by isolating the line, so that call happens immediately. The magnitude-5.1 aftershock is over, but its consequences cannot simply wait until tomorrow: occupied or shored buildings with known vulnerabilities need rapid re-checks before restrictions are relaxed. The gym decision already has a stable technical answer and can be communicated without consuming the field team. Good prioritisation stops the growing hazard while parallel work covers consequences with high life-safety stakes.
assumes: a problem still growing is different from one that has finished
why_this_format: The updated scene gives exactly what DELEGATE needs: a finite team, one condition still worsening, one completed event with life-safety consequences to check, and one loud deadline whose technical answer is already stable. A priority list is not enough. The player must turn each incident into owned work with a first move and a condition for coming back, while keeping personal attention on the consequence that needs engineering judgment.
player_does: choose which of the three incidents to keep personally
assign the other incidents to named functional owners with an immediate first action
set a return condition for every handoff so “watch it” is not accepted as a plan
trap_is_satisfied_by: The burst main is the only problem authored as both rising and effectively irreversible on the response timescale: every additional minute can add water to already susceptible fill before another aftershock. The school deadline is loud but stable because its technical conclusion is already established.

problems.label: Burst water main over liquefaction-susceptible fill
problems.firstAction: Order immediate isolation of the main and confirm flow is stopping
problems.returnCondition: Report when flow is isolated and the affected ground zone is marked for geotechnical check
problems.rate: still flowing, into the fill that liquefied a week ago
problems.consequence: pore pressure keeps rising under houses people are sleeping in until somebody closes the valve

problems.label: Known vulnerable occupied or shored buildings after the M5.1 aftershock
problems.firstAction: Start rapid re-checks at the highest-risk occupied or shored buildings
problems.returnCondition: Do not relax restrictions until the rapid re-checks show whether new distress occurred
problems.rate: not growing — the shaking is over, and eleven shored buildings are waiting on it
problems.consequence: restrictions come off occupied buildings on evidence gathered before the aftershock

problems.label: Bay Road School reopening communication deadline
problems.firstAction: Issue the already-supported classroom-open / gym-closed decision and route controls
problems.returnCondition: Return only if the isolation plan cannot keep occupied routes clear of the gym hazard
problems.rate: fixed at five o’clock; the technical answer has not moved since Tuesday
problems.consequence: a decision that is already made arrives late, or arrives from nobody

answerText: Keep the aftershock consequence checks under direct engineering attention, order the utility to isolate the burst main immediately, and hand the school communication to a desk engineer with the existing technical decision. Each handoff needs an owner, a first action and a condition for coming back; “watch it” is not a response plan.

failure_feedback.action: sending the whole team to the school deadline
failure_feedback.consequence: a stable communication problem consumes the field capacity while water continues entering susceptible ground and vulnerable buildings wait for post-aftershock checks
failure_feedback.line: The deadline is loud. The water is still moving.

dayTitle: Three things at once
title: Wetting ground that has already failed
task: Say what water does to fill
scene: Mbeki is on Ferry Street with a standpipe. The water table under the road has risen three quarters of a metre since the main went, and the ground surface is soft again underfoot.
question: Why does the burst main matter more here than it would in Upper Town?
takeaway: Raising the water table reduces effective stress in susceptible fill, increasing liquefaction susceptibility during renewed shaking without causing liquefaction by itself.
why: Soil skeleton strength comes from effective stress at grain contacts. Raising the groundwater level increases pore-water pressure and can reduce that effective stress in the loose fill before the next shaking starts. That does not mean the street liquefies merely because the pipe bursts; cyclic loading is still required. It does mean the margin against renewed pore-pressure buildup can shrink in susceptible layers. On competent granite the same water leak creates infrastructure problems, but not this liquefaction mechanism.
assumes: liquefaction requires saturated ground

dayTitle: Three things at once
title: A smaller shake against a weaker building
task: Work out what the 5.1 did to the shored buildings
scene: The 5.1 was about a tenth of the mainshock's ground motion in the Flats. Eleven buildings have been shored since Friday, and two of them have new cracking this afternoon.
question: What do the two buildings with new cracking tell the office?
takeaway: New cracking during a smaller aftershock is evidence that residual capacity or detailing deserves escalation; it is not a complete diagnosis by itself.
why: Shoring is temporary load support, not restoration of the damaged structural system. New cracking during a smaller aftershock therefore matters: it shows that the current combination of residual capacity, shoring and aftershock demand produced additional distress. That is a reason to maintain or tighten restrictions and perform a focused reassessment before deciding on strengthening, evacuation or a revised shore scheme. It does not by itself prove the shoring failed, identify the exact damaged mechanism, or tell you how close the building is to collapse.
assumes: a shored building is being held rather than repaired

dayTitle: The last morning it can be changed
title: Fixing the ground instead of the building
task: Say what ground improvement actually does
scene: Navarro has three options costed: stone columns, deep densification, and doing nothing to the ground while designing stiffer foundations on top of it.
question: What is the engineering difference between treating the ground and designing the foundation around the hazard?
takeaway: Ground improvement reduces liquefaction susceptibility or its consequences; structural foundations can instead bypass or accommodate some ground deformation.
why: The two strategies act at different places in the system. Densification can increase density and cyclic resistance; drains or stone columns may also help dissipate excess pore pressure, depending on the design. That reduces liquefaction susceptibility rather than guaranteeing the soil can never liquefy. Structural solutions such as piles or rafts may bypass weak layers or tolerate differential movement, but they leave roads, buried utilities and neighbouring sites exposed to ground deformation. Both can be legitimate; the town-level question is which consequences the policy is trying to reduce.
assumes: liquefaction can be addressed in the ground or accommodated in the structure

dayTitle: The last morning it can be changed
title: A measurable acceptance target
task: Quantify the change in cone resistance without turning it into a false safety factor
scene: Ferreira has cone penetration results from a trial panel: the fill tested at 4 MPa before the stone columns went in and 11 after.
question: By what factor did the measured cone resistance increase?
takeaway: CPT resistance is a measurable quality-control indicator; a 2.75-fold increase in qc is not automatically a 2.75-fold increase in liquefaction resistance.
why: The measured cone resistance rose from 4 to 11 MPa, a factor of 2.75. That is a strong, auditable construction-control result: the treated ground is substantially more resistant to penetration at that location. But qc is an input to liquefaction evaluation, not a direct safety factor. Cyclic resistance also depends on overburden, fines, groundwater and the design method used. A good specification can therefore require a target corrected CPT resistance or verified performance profile without claiming that '2.75 times qc' means '2.75 times safer.'
assumes: a cone test measures the resistance of ground to penetration

dayTitle: The last morning it can be changed
title: What the next five years hold
task: Commit, and say what the commitment contains
scene: The clause goes in or it does not, and it cannot be reopened for five years. Delacroix wants to know what each version means for somebody rebuilding next spring.
question: Commit, and say what the commitment contains
takeaway: Science can define the hazard and performance target; the rebuilding policy must also specify affordability, phasing and who carries the cost.
why: The engineering evidence can say what risk the loose fill creates and what performance a treatment programme should demonstrate. It cannot by itself decide who pays or how quickly households must comply. A requirement without financing can freeze rebuilding; no requirement can lock the same ground vulnerability into the next generation of streets and utilities. The strongest policy therefore states a measurable geotechnical performance target, defines where it applies, provides a funding or phasing mechanism, and includes a process for revisiting the rule as monitoring and new site data accumulate.
assumes: a decision to require something is also a decision about who pays for it

dayTitle: What we know, and how well
title: Measured, inferred, assumed
task: Sort the findings by their evidence
scene: Cardoso lays out four of the fortnight's statements. The office believes all four. They are not held for the same reasons and she will not let them into the report as equals.
question: Sort the findings by their evidence
takeaway: Sorting findings by their evidence is what lets a later reader know which ones to check first.
why: The four claims deserve different labels because their evidence chains differ. The vault siting error is directly documented and independently checked against competent rock. The hospital's 0.31 g is a direct measurement for one location and one event. Marina Court's mechanism is a strong inference from survey, ejecta and geotechnical behaviour rather than a direct observation beneath the raft. Future Flats amplification is conditional on corrected site-response evidence and the frequency content of a future earthquake. Stating those limits makes the report more useful, not weaker.
assumes: a claim can rest on a measurement, on an inference, or on nothing yet

dayTitle: What we know, and how well
title: The number that has to be a range
task: State the forecast as a range
scene: Tanaka's aftershock forecast goes into the report. She wants the range in the sentence and Okonkwo wants to know what the range is for.
question: Why does the forecast go in as a range rather than a single number?
takeaway: A forecast without a range cannot size a decision, because the decision is sized against the range.
why: Nobody staffs an emergency to the average week. They staff it to a week that is worse than average, and how much worse is exactly what the range says. A single number tells a planner nothing about how far the sequence might run above it, so the planner invents a margin — usually badly, usually too small. The range is also the honest part: it says which part of the behaviour is well constrained by four hundred recorded events and which is not.
assumes: a forecast is a distribution rather than a single value

dayTitle: What we know, and how well
title: What outlives the emergency
task: Choose the permanent practice that closes the repeated blind spot
scene: Four things the office started doing under pressure. Okonkwo asks which of them is worth its cost on an ordinary Tuesday, when nothing has happened.
question: Which permanent practice would most directly prevent the school, hospital and Ferry Street failure mode from repeating?
takeaway: An unknown only becomes safer when it has an owner, a deadline and a rule that prevents final clearance from silently forgetting it.
why: Whitcombe already wrote down what he could not inspect. The school gym, hospital plant room and Ferry Street basement were all on that second list; the failure was that nobody was required to close them. The durable practice is a formal unresolved-items register tied to occupancy: critical inaccessible areas get an owner and deadline, and final clearance cannot silently expire the task. Two engineers on every rapid placard halves throughput without targeting this failure. Daily meetings and blanket magnitude triggers are emergency tools, not permanent close-out systems.
assumes: a practice adopted under pressure has a cost that only shows later
